title: 'My treatment was a miracle,' says stroke patient as new 24-hour service rolled out
content:
When Gemma O'Hara woke up in the night with "intense pain" in her neck, sickness and vertigo she knew something was "not right".
The 40-year-old, who had just come back from holiday, had suffered a brain stem stroke.
Gemma was able to have a thrombectomy, which removes blood clots and restores blood flow to the brain, a procedure she has said is a "miracle treatment" that has enabled her to recover well.
Northern Ireland's regional thrombectomy service, which had only been available between 08:00 and 17:00 is now operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week after a £5m investment through Stormont's Programme for Government (PfG) Elective Care funding.
Gemma, from Ballymena in County Antrim, said the expansion is "amazing" because of the difference the treatment made to her recovery.
"You have to get treated so fast. You can't let time go past when it's to do with your brain," she said.
"If I didn't get it in time I wouldn't be the way I am now."
The mother-of three had the stroke in September 2025 and said that, while her symptoms were not classic stroke symptoms, she knew she needed medical help.
By the time she arrived at the Antrim Area Hospital, she had numbness, could not walk or talk and felt "locked in my body".
She was scanned and given thrombolysis - clot-busting medication - before being transferred to the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast for a thrombectomy.
Gemma said that within minutes of having her procedure she was "sitting up, back to myself again" and waiting for her family to arrive.
"It's a miracle treatment because I was so unwell and for something that can happen fairly quickly like that, and to recover so well, it's amazing," she said.
She said having a stroke was "so unexpected".
"I was always working, going to the gym and trying to look after myself.
"So for everybody that was a big shock for me to have a stroke because they always thought I would have been the fittest one."
Gemma said one of her "biggest fears" had been the possibly of having another stroke during the night, when thrombectomy was previously unavailable.
She said the 24/7 service gives her "peace of mind" that she would be able to receive treatment if it happened again.
The expanded service, which began on 14 September, means the time of day or night a stroke occurs is no longer a barrier to accessing treatment.
Dr Patricia Gordon, stroke consultant at Belfast Health Trust, said about 10% of patients who have a stroke have a large clot that can be removed through a thrombectomy.
She said the procedure increases a patient's chances of making a good recovery by more than 50% and reduces the risk of death by almost 20%.

title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
content:
President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was watching closely amid concerns the incident could lead to the spread of pneumonic plague, but there was no cause for alarm.
Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".
Unconfirmed reports suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
Asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague spreading from Russia, Trump said he had not spoken to the Kremlin about it.
"I hate to see them having it," he said, but added: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help."
No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since the lab technician's death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.
The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.
Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.
Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature.
"If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."
The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.
The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis , which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death , is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East was founded just over 100 years ago.
Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.
"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."

title: Nobel Prize awarded for revealing inner workings of the brain
content:
US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in the field of optogenetics.
Their research has helped scientists learn more about the inner workings of the brain, to better understand how the human mind works.
The Nobel Committee praised the trio for laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience by revealing how to switch on and off neural circuits behind "specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders".
In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method to try to restore sight in people with visual impairment .
"Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain," the Nobel Assembly said.
"Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity's great mysteries: how our incredible brain works."
The winners said it was "absolutely wonderful" to get the award, and that it was an honour to share the accolade with friends.
The three men will also share the £900,000 (12 million Swedish kronor) prize money.
Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, explained: "Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."
Before, the inner workings behind feelings, behaviours and bodily functions were more of a mystery to scientists.
Optogenetics is a way to illuminate brain pathways, using a special protein borrowed from algae that scientists use to control cell electrical activity using light.
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, the algal protein with unique properties.
Deisseroth worked out how to use this light controlled protein to switch on nerve cells in the brains of mice.
Researchers have since been able to study nerve cells and pathways in animals to see and discover more about what they do.
The Nobel Committee said: "Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in the brain. They can bring memories to life, create feelings, drive behaviours and study the types of neurons that are involved in various psychiatric and neurological disorders."
That is providing important insights into how the nervous system interacts with various cells in other areas of the body, such as in the heart and gut, the committee added.
Researchers have also taken "the first steps" towards using optogenetics as a medical treatment, the committee explained.
In ongoing clinical trials, scientists have been working to restore vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye's rods and cones.
By inserting a special protein in the damaged region of the eye, the patient regained some vision when wearing special glasses emitting light. This switched on the therapeutic algae proteins.
Further details have been released showing how the new 30-storey hospital may look, if plans go ahead.
